steps.title: Text A · What everybody knows
steps.html:
Written for this course.

Everybody knows the descriptions. Born between 1965 and 1980, Gen X are easy-going, family-focused and deeply suspicious of employers. Gen Y are fussy about who they work for, enthusiastic about the work itself and unimpressed by job titles. Gen Z, arriving last, are said to be either the most rebellious cohort in decades or the most conventional, depending on which article you happen to be reading; keen on stable jobs, optimistic about their own lives and pessimistic about everything else, they are described in terms that are supposed to be characteristic of a generation raised online. Asked to describe themselves, members of all three groups reach for the same words: open-minded, realistic, hard-working. Asked about the group below them, they become noticeably less generous, producing self-centred and arrogant within about a minute.

There is a labelling problem underneath all of this. Described by a manager who is sympathetic towards them, a young employee asking for feedback is self-confident; described by one who is not, the same employee is arrogant. Keen on flexible hours, they are either realistic about modern life or not loyal enough, and which of those you write down says more about you than about them.

We associate impatience with the young because we stop noticing it in ourselves, and the same answer, given by a twenty-year-old, is coded differently from the way it is coded when a fifty-year-old gives it. None of this is deliberate. It is what happens when a category is available and a judgement has to be made quickly, and it is the reason the descriptions in the first paragraph feel so obviously true to almost everybody who reads them.

steps.title: Text B · What the evidence shows
steps.html:
Written for this course, from Costanza, Badger, Fraser, Severt & Gade, Journal of Business and Psychology 27(4), 2012.

Being confident about something is not the same as being right about it. In 2012 a team of researchers collected twenty published and unpublished studies covering nearly twenty thousand employees, comparing four generations on three things that organisations actually care about: job satisfaction, commitment to the employer, and intention to leave. Combining the studies statistically, they found differences that were small to moderate and, in many of the comparisons, essentially zero. Their conclusion was blunt: meaningful generational differences in these attitudes probably do not exist.

Understanding why the belief survives means separating three things that a single survey cannot separate. The first is age: people are different at twenty-five from how they are at fifty, whatever year they were born. The second is period — a recession or a housing crisis hits everybody at once, regardless of cohort. The third is generation proper. Run a survey in one year and all three arrive tangled together, and the tidiest explanation is usually the one that gets printed. The categories are also commercially useful, which is a different thing from being accurate: a birth year is easier to sell than a personality, and, having been repeated for thirty years, the labels now feel like observations rather than inventions.

What survives the criticism is modest but real. Shared events do shape people, and somebody who left university in 2009 entered a labour market that somebody leaving in 2006 never saw. But the boundaries are arbitrary — December 1980 and January 1981 are not two different worlds — and the variation inside any generation is far larger than the gap between them. Taken seriously, the research does not say that people are all alike. It says the dividing line is almost certainly not the year of birth.

Text A · What everybody knows

Written for this course.

Everybody knows the descriptions. Born between 1965 and 1980, Gen X are easy-going, family-focused and deeply suspicious of employers. Gen Y are fussy about who they work for, enthusiastic about the work itself and unimpressed by job titles. Gen Z, arriving last, are said to be either the most rebellious cohort in decades or the most conventional, depending on which article you happen to be reading; keen on stable jobs, optimistic about their own lives and pessimistic about everything else, they are described in terms that are supposed to be characteristic of a generation raised online. Asked to describe themselves, members of all three groups reach for the same words: open-minded, realistic, hard-working. Asked about the group below them, they become noticeably less generous, producing self-centred and arrogant within about a minute.

There is a labelling problem underneath all of this. Described by a manager who is sympathetic towards them, a young employee asking for feedback is self-confident; described by one who is not, the same employee is arrogant. Keen on flexible hours, they are either realistic about modern life or not loyal enough, and which of those you write down says more about you than about them.

We associate impatience with the young because we stop noticing it in ourselves, and the same answer, given by a twenty-year-old, is coded differently from the way it is coded when a fifty-year-old gives it. None of this is deliberate. It is what happens when a category is available and a judgement has to be made quickly, and it is the reason the descriptions in the first paragraph feel so obviously true to almost everybody who reads them.

Text B · What the evidence shows

Written for this course, from Costanza, Badger, Fraser, Severt & Gade, Journal of Business and Psychology 27(4), 2012.

Being confident about something is not the same as being right about it. In 2012 a team of researchers collected twenty published and unpublished studies covering nearly twenty thousand employees, comparing four generations on three things that organisations actually care about: job satisfaction, commitment to the employer, and intention to leave. Combining the studies statistically, they found differences that were small to moderate and, in many of the comparisons, essentially zero. Their conclusion was blunt: meaningful generational differences in these attitudes probably do not exist.

Understanding why the belief survives means separating three things that a single survey cannot separate. The first is age: people are different at twenty-five from how they are at fifty, whatever year they were born. The second is period — a recession or a housing crisis hits everybody at once, regardless of cohort. The third is generation proper. Run a survey in one year and all three arrive tangled together, and the tidiest explanation is usually the one that gets printed. The categories are also commercially useful, which is a different thing from being accurate: a birth year is easier to sell than a personality, and, having been repeated for thirty years, the labels now feel like observations rather than inventions.

What survives the criticism is modest but real. Shared events do shape people, and somebody who left university in 2009 entered a labour market that somebody leaving in 2006 never saw. But the boundaries are arbitrary — December 1980 and January 1981 are not two different worlds — and the variation inside any generation is far larger than the gap between them. Taken seriously, the research does not say that people are all alike. It says the dividing line is almost certainly not the year of birth.
steps.prompt: Combining the studies statistically, they found differences that were essentially zero. ____
options: When they combined the studies statistically
Because the studies were combined by somebody else
The studies, which were combined statistically
steps.answer: When they combined the studies statistically
steps.why: The participle’s subject must match the main clause subject — the researchers.

steps.title: -ing, -ed, and having + participle
steps.html:
How to say the same thing in fewer words — and the one rule you must not break.

A participle clause replaces a full clause and drops the subject and the auxiliary. Because they grew up in a period of rising wages, they are confident → Having grown up in a period of rising wages, they are confident.

-ing (present participle) has an active meaning and usually means while, because or and: Growing up with smart devices, they are tech-savvy.

-ed (past participle) has a passive meaning: Asked to describe their own generation, people rarely use those words = when they are asked.

Having + past participle makes it clear the first action came earlier: Having entered work during a recession, they are cautious.

The rule you must not break: the participle and the main clause must share the same subject. Looking at the four descriptions, something becomes obvious is technically loose, because something is not doing the looking — writers allow it, but Walking home, the rain started is simply wrong: the rain was not walking.

Participle clauses are a written form. They make a text denser and more formal, which is why the two texts in this lesson are full of them and a conversation would not be.

Having entered work during a recession, it is financially careful.

Simultaneous.

never having known a world without them

Common in writing, though the subjects do not strictly match.

Passive: when they are asked.

Researchers working on this have made the point for thirty years.

steps.title: Reducing a full clause in three steps
steps.html:
1. The full version: Because Generation Y entered work during a recession, it is financially careful.
  2. Check the subjects match. Generation Y entered, and it is careful — the same thing. Good; a participle clause is allowed.
  3. Drop the conjunction and the subject, and put the verb into a participle. The entering came first, so use having + past participle: Having entered work during a recession, it is financially careful.
  4. If the action were simultaneous instead, use plain -ing: Growing up with smart devices, it is tech-savvy. If it were passive, use the past participle: Asked about it, it says nothing.
  5. Now break the rule to see it: Having entered work during a recession, the labels are unfair. The labels did not enter work. That sentence is wrong.

steps.title: Write your piece.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Use at least four participle clauses, including one with having and one passive.
steps.html:
• Open with dates and the usual description, using a passive participle.
  • Explain the cause with <i>Having</i> + past participle.
  • Use <i>Asked…</i> or another passive participle for what they say themselves.
  • Close by separating the group from the individual.

Useful language

  • Born between … and … , they are usually described as …
  • Having grown up in a period of … , they are …
  • Growing up with … , we never …
  • Asked about it, most of them …
  • Used carefully, the label describes …
  • It is characteristic of / associated with …
steps.modelHtml:
The people who remember the queues

Born between about 1955 and 1970, my parents' generation is usually described as cautious, hard-working and slightly suspicious of anybody who promises something for nothing. Having spent their twenties in a system that collapsed, they are not enthusiastic about being told that the next arrangement is permanent.

Asked to describe themselves, they say none of this. They say they were lucky, and they list the things they had that we do not.

Growing up in the nineties, I watched them keep every receipt and never once carry a balance on a card. That is not meanness. It is a habit formed by a decade in which money genuinely stopped meaning what it had meant.

Used carefully, the label describes what they lived through. Applied to my mother, who is the least cautious person I know, it describes nothing.
